one_liner: Small C++20 work-stealing thread pool on Chase-Lev deques; about 8% faster than BS::thread_pool in one third-party matmul benchmark.
what_it_does: A header-only thread pool, riften::Thiefpool. enqueue(f, args...) returns a std::future, and enqueue_detach(f, args...) runs a void callable without allocating a future's shared state. Arguments are copied, as with std::async. The destructor requests stop and joins the std::jthread workers. The interface is close to BS::thread_pool's submit, but it is not source-compatible and has no wait_for_tasks, parallel-loop or pause helpers.
how_it_is_fast: Each worker owns a lock-free riften::Deque (Chase-Lev work-stealing deque) of fu2::unique_function tasks, a move-only type-erased function with small-buffer storage. Tasks are dealt round-robin to the deques, and a lightweight semaphore (adapted from Preshing's) wakes the target worker. Workers take from their own deque first; after 100 spins with their own deque empty they steal from a random deque (xoroshiro128**). They keep spinning while a global in-flight counter is above zero. enqueue avoids std::packaged_task type erasure by using a NullaryOneShot wrapper.
when_to_use: A single producer thread submits many small, independent tasks and wants lower per-task overhead than a mutex-and-condition-variable pool such as BS::thread_pool.
Fire-and-forget jobs where enqueue_detach skips the std::future allocation.
C++20 codebases using CPM.cmake that want a tiny pool (one header plus function2 and riften::Deque).
Coarse parallel chunks (e.g. 256x256 to 1024x1024 matmul tiles) where it measured 52.80 vs 57.14 ms/op against BS::thread_pool.
when_not_to_use: Submitting from several threads or from inside tasks: execute() bumps a non-atomic counter and calls the deque's owner-only emplace from the caller's thread. That is a data race unless one thread does all the enqueuing (open issue #4, no maintainer reply).
Tasks that block on or depend on later tasks: a worker can go back to sleep while another worker's deque holds a pending task (open issue #2, 'Deadlock due to lack of cross thread signalling').
Latency- or power-sensitive services: woken workers busy-spin and steal until the global in-flight count reaches zero.
Fork-join or recursive parallelism: there is no task-local spawn/join; choose libfork, chili or Fork Union style schedulers.
Small-task workloads where dp::thread_pool or task_thread_pool measured faster (e.g. 8x8 matmul: 172.33 ms vs task_thread_pool 154.74 ms). The project has been abandoned since 2023-03-26.

integration.dependencies: function2 (Naios/function2 4.1.0), riften::Deque (ConorWilliams/ConcurrentDeque v1.1.0), Threads; fetched via CPM.cmake
integration.platforms: any with C++20 threads; the semaphore has Windows, macOS and POSIX backends
integration.thread_safety: Workers are concurrent, but enqueue/enqueue_detach are safe only from a single thread (non-atomic round-robin counter; Chase-Lev push is owner-only). Not documented in the README.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: future-returning enqueue similar to BS::thread_pool::submit, but no wait-all, parallel loops, pause or resize, and no multi-producer submission

gotchas: The in-flight counter is decremented before a task runs, so workers sleep while a long task is still executing. A task enqueued to that busy worker's deque waits for it to finish (issue #2).
Exceptions from enqueue tasks go into the std::future. An exception thrown by an enqueue_detach task escapes the worker thread and calls std::terminate (no try/catch in the worker loop).
Each deque keeps every buffer it outgrows in a _garbage vector until the pool is destroyed, so memory after a burst is not returned.
MPL-2.0: file-level copyleft; modified pool files must stay MPL.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over BS::thread_pool-style pools only when one thread submits many independent tasks and the C++20 dependency is fine. dp::thread_pool measured 1-2% faster in the same benchmark and is maintained, and Fork Union or citor are the better choice for parallel-for or fork-join throughput.
verified_claims_summary: The only numbers come from dp::thread_pool's own nanobench matrix-multiplication comparison on a Ryzen 7 5800X (Windows, Clang via WSL and MSVC, flags not stated). Thiefpool scored 98.3-99.0% of dp::thread_pool versus 90.2-94.5% for BS::thread_pool (1024x1024: 52.80 vs 57.14 ms/op, about 8% faster, derived from page data), and it trailed task_thread_pool at 8x8 to 256x256. The repo's own bench.cpp (10M enqueues of an atomic increment, three workloads) publishes no results.
status_note: Abandoned: last commit 2023-03-26, v2.1.1, two open concurrency issues (#2, #4) with no maintainer reply. It is small enough to vendor under MPL-2.0 if you keep submission on one thread.
